title: First words
goal: Greet people politely, say yes and no, thank someone, apologise and ask how someone is.
intro:
Welcome to Hindi! In this unit you'll learn the words you'll use every single day: hello, yes, no, thanks, sorry. You'll also meet the most important social idea in Hindi grammar: there are **three words for 'you'**, depending on how respectful or close you are.

Don't worry about reading the script fast yet — use the romanization, listen, and repeat out loud.

vocab.en: hello; goodbye (respectful, any time of day)
vocab.note: Said with palms pressed together. Works for hello and goodbye.

grammar.title: Word order: the verb comes last
grammar.body:
English says *I am fine*; Hindi says **मैं ठीक हूँ** — literally 'I fine am'. Hindi is a **subject–object–verb** (SOV) language: the verb (here हूँ 'am') goes at the end, and everything else comes before it.

Subject – (object / description) – verb
मैं – ठीक – हूँ

Questions use the same order. You can turn a statement into a yes/no question just by raising your voice at the end, or by putting **क्या** at the front. Question words like कैसे 'how' usually go right before the verb.

examples.en: Are you OK? (kyā you fine are)

grammar.title: Three ways to say 'you': आप, तुम, तू
grammar.body:
Hindi chooses its 'you' by **respect and closeness**, and the verb changes with it:

**आप** *āp* — respectful: strangers, elders, teachers, shopkeepers, in-laws, anyone in a formal setting. Verb: **हैं** *haiṃ*.
**तुम** *tum* — familiar: friends your age, younger relatives, children, partners. Verb: **हो** *ho*.
**तू** *tū* — intimate or rude: best friends, small children, prayers. Verb: **है** *hai*.

When in doubt, use **आप** — nobody is offended by too much respect. Adding **जी** makes almost anything more polite: जी हाँ 'yes (respectfully)', and after a name, रवि जी 'Ravi-ji'.

Note also that कैसा 'how' changes its ending: कैसे for men (and for the respectful आप), कैसी for women.

examples.en: How are you? (familiar, to a man/boy)
How are you? (familiar, to a woman/girl)
How are you? (intimate, to a close male friend)

dialogue.title: Meeting a neighbour
dialogue.setting: Ravi meets his new neighbour, Mrs Sharma, on the stairs in the morning.

lines.speaker: Ravi
lines.native: मैं ठीक हूँ, शुक्रिया। और आप?
lines.roman: maiṃ ṭhīk hūṃ, shukriyā. aur āp?

lines.speaker: Mrs Sharma
lines.native: मैं भी ठीक हूँ। आपसे मिलकर ख़ुशी हुई।
lines.roman: maiṃ bhī ṭhīk hūṃ. āpse milkar xushī huī.
lines.en: I'm fine too. Nice to meet you.

lines.speaker: Ravi
lines.native: जी, मुझे भी। आपका स्वागत है!
lines.roman: jī, mujhe bhī. āpkā svāgat hai!

lines.speaker: Ravi
lines.native: अरे, माफ़ कीजिए, मैं जल्दी में हूँ।
lines.roman: are, māf kījiye, maiṃ jaldī meṃ hūṃ.
lines.en: Oh, sorry, I'm in a hurry.

culture: **नमस्ते** with palms pressed together and a slight nod is safe with everyone. You'll also hear greetings tied to community and region: **अस्सलाम अलैकुम** *assalām alaikum* among Muslims (reply **वालेकुम अस्सलाम**), **सत श्री अकाल** *sat shrī akāl* among Sikhs, and **राम-राम** or **जय श्री कृष्ण** in villages and among older Hindus. Touching an elder's feet is a sign of deep respect in families. Among close family and friends, saying 'thank you' too often can sound distant — warmth is shown by actions instead. Young urban speakers mix English freely: *hi, bye, sorry, thank you, OK* are all perfectly normal Hindi today.

tip.title: The verb goes last
tip.body:
- Hindi puts the verb at the **end**: मैं ठीक हूँ is literally 'I fine am'.
- **हूँ** = am (with मैं), **हैं** = are (with आप).
- Question words like **कैसे** 'how' sit just before the verb: आप कैसे हैं?

sentences.en: Hello, how are you? (to a man)
Hello, how are you? (to a woman)

sentences.native: मैं ठीक हूँ, आप कैसे हैं?
sentences.roman: maiṃ ṭhīk hūṃ, āp kaise haiṃ?

tip.title: Yes/no questions with क्या
tip.body:
- Put **क्या** at the front and a statement becomes a yes/no question: आप ठीक हैं → **क्या** आप ठीक हैं?
- **नहीं** 'not' goes right before the verb: मैं ठीक **नहीं** हूँ.
- **भी** 'too' comes *after* the word it belongs to: मैं **भी** 'me too'.
- Add **जी** for politeness: जी हाँ, जी नहीं.

sentences.native: जी नहीं, मैं ठीक नहीं हूँ।
sentences.roman: jī nahīṃ, maiṃ ṭhīk nahīṃ hūṃ.

tip.title: Three ways to say "you"
tip.body:
- **आप** (respectful) → verb **हैं**: strangers, elders, shopkeepers. When unsure, use आप.
- **तुम** (friendly) → verb **हो**: friends your age, younger people.
- **तू** (very close) → verb **है**: best friends only. As a learner, you mostly hear it.
- कैसे changes too: कैसा (one man, with तू), कैसी (a woman), कैसे (आप/तुम, a man).
tip.pattern: आप … हैं  ·  तुम … हो  ·  तू … है

sentences.en: How are you? (to a male friend)
How are you? (to a female friend)
How are you? (to a close male friend)

sentences.native: आप कैसे हैं, और तुम कैसे हो?
sentences.roman: āp kaise haiṃ, aur tum kaise ho?
sentences.en: How are you (sir), and how are you (friend)?

tip.title: Politeness without "please"
tip.body:
- **कृपया** 'please' is mostly for signs and announcements. In speech, politeness comes from **जी** and polite verb forms like **कीजिए**.
- **शुक्रिया** is the everyday 'thanks'; **धन्यवाद** is more formal. Many people simply say *thank you*.
- **माफ़ कीजिए** = 'excuse me / I'm sorry'. Casual: **सॉरी**. The reply: **कोई बात नहीं** 'no problem'.

sentences.native: माफ़ कीजिए, क्या आप ठीक हैं?
sentences.roman: māf kījie, kyā āp ṭhīk haiṃ?

sentences.native: कोई बात नहीं, सब ठीक है।
sentences.roman: koī bāt nahīṃ, sab ṭhīk hai.

lessons.title: Nice to meet you, see you again

tip.title: Hellos and goodbyes
tip.body:
- **नमस्ते** works for both hello and goodbye, any time of day. **नमस्कार** is a little more formal.
- To part: **फिर मिलेंगे** 'see you again', or just *bye* (**बाय**). **अलविदा** is dramatic, like 'farewell'.
- **आपसे मिलकर ख़ुशी हुई** = 'nice to meet you' (lit. having met you, happiness happened).
